doc.title: Carmen Caramanica interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, July 27, 2011

title: Teaching ear training versus tablature, singing what you play
summary: Students who download tabs do not develop ear; he has them sing notes, and tells of grunting while playing on a recording session.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: I love those behind-the-scenes stories. And some of those skills, I mean I was thinking about the way you and I learned music, with our ear to the radio or to the record player, and these copyists doing that stuff. I will now sound old-fashioned, but those ways of learning are not around anymore that much.

No. And it’s too bad because people are losing a valuable skill. I teach guitar, and a lot of my students, if they want to learn a tune they go to the Internet and they download a tab [tablature], all right? So the music is not all music, but just numbers. But anyway, they listen to it, they see the numbers and they do that. And then they don’t really develop any kind of ear, any kind of relative pitch, so they can’t figure stuff out on their own, and then they say “I don’t need to I can get the tab.” And if it isn’t out today it’ll be out tomorrow, I’ll get it. And so where’s the development? Where is that whole thing? And it impedes their ability to improvise, see, especially on guitar, you’ve got the problem is we have patterns, and it’s very visual. So when you first learn to improvise on the blues is where we start most kids that want to do that, they learn to put these little pentatonic patterns on the keyboard, on the fingerboard. And it’s two notes on each string. And we’ll say well okay mix them up. So they just kind of run up and down the scale and it kind of sounds like it works if you put a background track to it. But it takes a while before they begin to realize what the function of each one of those notes is, how it relates to the chord, when you should use the third, when you should go to something else. And they don’t see this because they just look at the pattern and run it over and over and over again. Now when you try to compose something you have to like listen to what’s going on in your mind and play what you’re hearing, without hearing anything. They’re just “oh that’s what that sounds like, I see.” And so you have to kind of go backwards and say well look, let’s take a song you’ve never heard before, or that you’ve never played before. Let’s do “Yankee Doodle.” Put your first finger here. And now find the next three notes. And a lot of them © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -11-

really don’t know which way is up, which way is down. So we say “try singing the note when you’re playing it.” Okay. So they’ll play and sing the first note and then “what’s the next note?” and you make them sing it, and now where is that, it’s over here. And so by doing this they start to sing what they play. And this goes back to another war story, which is when I first discovered that was a good way to develop the brain-instrument relationship so you’re really playing what you’re hearing not just what you think is going to sound good, you have to hear it first then play it, I sang everything. And it got to be a habit. Now if you’ve heard me sing, it’s kind of like my writing, you don’t want to hear much of it. So by playing and singing at the same time I was definitely connecting with my musical self inside the brain. But it got to the point where I was singing pretty loud while I was playing. And actually one time Rick Montalbano and I were doing a recording session and I was next to the piano, and we were playing and then we stopped and he said “hey you want to stop?” I said “stop what?” He says “you’re grunting every note that you play and it’s going to get into the mic of the piano.” And he was right I was [grunts] doing that. And I know I kind of still do that today because sometimes I’ll play a set and I’ll get off and I feel hoarse because it’s coming out.
